records.name: Map is Not the Territory

origin.author: Alfred Korzybski
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Any model, map or metric is a simplification that leaves things out. Check it against what is actually happening before acting on it, and notice when the conditions it was built for have changed.
records.key_question: What does my model leave out that reality contains?
use_when: decisions driven by dashboards, reports or proxy metrics
credentials or specs standing in for demonstrated ability
records.produces: list of omitted variables and where the model breaks
records.failure_mode: Used to reject every model as inadequate, producing paralysis instead of a better map.

records.name: Circle of Competence

origin.author: Warren Buffett
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Know the areas where your judgment has a track record and where it does not. Inside them, act; outside them, slow down, borrow expertise or stay out.
records.key_question: Is this inside my circle, and what is the evidence that it is?
use_when: high confidence with thin track record
evaluating advice from outside the speaker's field
records.produces: explicit in/out boundary plus who to consult outside it
records.failure_mode: Used as permanent justification for never entering a new domain.

records.name: First Principles Thinking

origin.author: Aristotle
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Strip a problem down to what is known to be true, discarding convention and analogy, then reason upward from there. Useful when the usual approach is assumed rather than justified.
records.key_question: What is actually true here once convention, analogy and inherited process are stripped out?
records.produces: irreducible constraint set and the solution space it permits
records.failure_mode: Rebuilding systems whose conventions encode hard-won knowledge you have not yet recovered.

records.name: Thought Experiment

origin.author: Galileo; Albert Einstein
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Run the scenario in your head: change one variable, imagine the outcome, follow it through. Exposes hidden assumptions and consequences cheaply, before testing anything in the world.
records.key_question: If I run this to its logical limit, what breaks and what becomes obvious?
use_when: real-world test is too costly or slow
records.produces: counterfactual scenarios and boundary conditions
records.failure_mode: Treating imagined results as data. A thought experiment generates hypotheses, never evidence.

records.name: Second-Order Thinking

origin.author: Howard Marks
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Look past the immediate result to the reactions it triggers: who responds, how, and what follows from their response. First effects are often the opposite of later ones.
records.key_question: Who reacts to this, and what happens after their reaction?
records.produces: consequence chain with named reacting actors
records.failure_mode: Speculative chains presented as forecast; infinite regress used to avoid deciding.

records.name: Probabilistic Thinking

origin.author: Thomas Bayes
origin.work: An Essay Towards Solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Treat outcomes as a range with likelihoods rather than as certain or impossible. Put rough numbers on them and revise those numbers as evidence arrives.
records.key_question: What are the odds, against what base rate, and what evidence would move them?
use_when: binary yes/no framing of an uncertain outcome
records.produces: calibrated estimate with explicit update triggers
records.failure_mode: False precision: a percentage with no reference class behind it is a feeling in numeric clothing.

records.name: Inversion

origin.author: Carl Jacobi
origin.work: Jacobi's maxim, popularised by Charlie Munger
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Approach the problem backwards: ask what would make it fail, or what you want to avoid, then steer away from that. Often clearer than asking directly how to succeed.
records.key_question: What would guarantee failure here, and am I doing any of it?
records.produces: ranked avoid-list of failure paths
records.failure_mode: Avoidance-only strategy that eliminates downside without ever building upside.

records.name: Occam's Razor

origin.author: William of Ockham
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Between explanations that fit the facts equally well, start with the one that needs the fewest extra assumptions. A default for ordering hypotheses, not proof that the simple one is right.
records.key_question: Which explanation requires the fewest unsupported assumptions?
records.produces: explanations ranked by assumption load
records.failure_mode: Amputating real complexity. Simplicity is a tiebreaker, not evidence of truth.

records.name: Hanlon's Razor

origin.author: Robert J. Hanlon
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Before concluding someone acted out of malice, check whether carelessness, ignorance or confusion would explain it. Those are far more common causes of harm.
records.key_question: Do incompetence, constraint or incentive explain this before malice does?
records.produces: alternative causal candidates ranked by prior likelihood
records.failure_mode: Excusing repeated, patterned harm that has already outrun the incompetence explanation.

records.name: Velocity

origin.author: Classical mechanics
origin.work: Speed versus velocity as a vector
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Velocity is speed with a direction. Moving fast toward the wrong goal is waste, so confirm where you are heading before working on how quickly you get there.
records.key_question: Has the direction been checked before we speed up?
records.produces: direction statement plus current rate toward it
records.failure_mode: Used to rationalise slowness as thoughtfulness.

records.name: Leverage

origin.author: Archimedes
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: A small input in the right place can move something much larger. Find the points where effort is multiplied, and remember that leverage magnifies losses as well as gains.
records.key_question: Where does one unit of my effort return ten?
records.produces: ranked leverage points with expected multiple
records.failure_mode: Leverage amplifies error identically to success; the downside tail is routinely ignored.

records.name: Activation Energy

origin.author: Svante Arrhenius
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Starting takes more effort than continuing. Lower the cost of the first step, or supply a burst of effort at the start, and the process can then sustain itself.
records.key_question: What is the minimum energy required to start, and who pays it?
records.produces: barrier-lowering actions
records.failure_mode: Starting many things cheaply and finishing none.

records.name: Alloying

origin.author: Metallurgy
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Combining ingredients in the right proportions can produce properties none of them has alone. Applied to skills or teams: an unusual mix can be worth more than depth in one area.
records.key_question: Which combination of ordinary components produces a rare and valuable whole?
records.produces: combination candidates with proportions
records.failure_mode: Mixing without proportion, producing a blend that is mediocre at everything.

records.name: Red Queen Effect

origin.author: Leigh Van Valen
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: When rivals keep improving, you have to improve just to hold your position. Standing still in a competitive environment means falling behind.
records.key_question: What must I improve simply to stay where I am?
records.produces: standstill requirement separated from real gains
records.failure_mode: Justifying permanent overwork; treating every competitive field as an arms race.

records.name: Ecosystems

origin.author: Arthur Tansley
origin.work: The Use and Abuse of Vegetational Concepts and Terms
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: An ecosystem is a web of interdependent parts. Intervening in one place has effects elsewhere, so map the connections before changing anything.
records.key_question: Who else is in this system, and what breaks if I move this piece?
records.produces: dependency and stakeholder map with intervention risks
records.failure_mode: Complexity worship: mapping forever as a substitute for acting.

records.name: Niches

origin.author: G. Evelyn Hutchinson
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Fitting a narrow environment well can beat competing broadly. A niche offers protection from rivals, but it is exposed if that environment changes.
records.key_question: Where am I the best available option rather than one option among many?
records.produces: defensible niche definition with its fragility conditions
records.failure_mode: A niche narrow enough to be safe today and extinct after one environmental shift.

records.name: Replication
records.evidence_note: Imitation of successful strategies is documented in social-learning and diffusion research. Copying fails when context differs, and survivorship hides the copiers that failed.

origin.author: Richard Dawkins
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Copying a proven approach is often faster and safer than inventing one. Replicate what works to get a reliable base, then improve on it.
records.key_question: Who has already solved this, and what precisely did they do?
records.produces: proven baseline to replicate before innovating
records.failure_mode: Copying a winner's visible traits without their unobserved conditions or luck.

records.name: Hierarchical Organization

origin.author: Herbert Simon
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Layered structures let a system scale and specialise, but each layer filters information and adds distance from reality. Check what the hierarchy is preventing as well as enabling.
records.key_question: Is this hierarchy serving coordination, or serving status competition?
records.produces: structural diagnosis and where levels are redundant
records.failure_mode: Blaming structure for problems caused by people, incentives or strategy.

records.name: Incentives
records.evidence_note: Incentives shift behaviour in many settings (Kerr 1975; field experiments). Rewards can also crowd out intrinsic motivation, so the direction and size of the effect vary.

origin.author: Charlie Munger
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: People respond to what they are rewarded and punished for, not to what they are asked to do. Map the actual incentives to explain behaviour, and expect gaming of any measure.
records.key_question: Who gets paid, promoted or protected by the current outcome?
use_when: policy that is ignored in practice
records.produces: incentive map with predicted behaviour per actor
records.failure_mode: Assuming perfectly rational response to incentives; people also misread their own payoffs.

records.name: Equilibrium

origin.author: Donella Meadows
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Many systems settle into a balance between opposing forces and return to it after small shocks. Know what holds the balance in place before trying to move it.
records.key_question: What opposing forces hold this steady, and which one must change?
records.produces: force balance with the binding force named
records.failure_mode: Assuming a stable state is either desirable or permanent.

records.name: Bottlenecks

origin.author: Eliyahu Goldratt
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: The output of a whole process is limited by its slowest step. Improving anything else adds no capacity, so locate the constraint first.
records.key_question: What single constraint sets the pace, and is everything else noise?
records.produces: identified constraint and focused plan on it alone
records.failure_mode: Relieving a bottleneck that simply relocates downstream, with no net gain.

records.name: Scale
records.evidence_note: Scaling laws (square-cube, urban and metabolic scaling) are empirical and fit well in their domains. They do not transfer to every organisation; check the exponent for your case.

origin.author: Galileo Galilei
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Growth changes the problem. What works for ten fails at a thousand, as costs, coordination and failure modes shift with size; each order of magnitude needs rethinking.
records.key_question: What breaks at 10x and at 100x?
records.produces: breakage list per order of magnitude
records.failure_mode: Designing for scale before the thing works at 1x.

records.name: Margin of Safety

origin.author: Benjamin Graham
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Build in more capacity than the expected load requires, to absorb errors and surprises. The buffer costs efficiency in normal times and pays off in bad ones.
records.key_question: What if I am wrong; how much buffer survives that?
records.produces: required buffer and its cost
records.failure_mode: Over-buffering into an uncompetitive cost structure; safety as an excuse for inaction.

records.name: Algorithms

origin.author: Donald Knuth
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: An algorithm is a fixed sequence of steps that turns inputs into outputs. Codifying a routine decision makes it fast and consistent, provided the conditions behind the rule still hold.
records.key_question: Can this decision be reduced to a rule I would trust while exhausted?
records.produces: explicit decision rule with its validity conditions
records.failure_mode: Rules applied long past the conditions that justified them.

records.name: Critical Mass

origin.author: Mark Granovetter
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Some changes do nothing until a threshold is crossed, then become self-sustaining. Find where the threshold lies and whether the effort is enough to reach it.
records.key_question: What threshold must be crossed before this sustains itself?
records.produces: threshold estimate and path to reach it
records.failure_mode: Assuming a threshold exists where the underlying growth is actually linear.

records.name: Irreducibility

origin.author: Stephen Wolfram
origin.work: A New Kind of Science (computational irreducibility)
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Some phenomena lose their essential character when broken into parts. When decomposition keeps failing, study the whole system rather than the pieces.
records.key_question: What cannot be broken down, shortened or outsourced without destroying the thing?
records.produces: irreducible core and the compressible remainder
records.failure_mode: Declaring something irreducible to shield it from scrutiny or measurement.

records.name: Law of Diminishing Returns

origin.author: Anne-Robert-Jacques Turgot; David Ricardo
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Beyond some point, each additional unit of effort yields less than the last. Recognise when the curve has flattened and redirect effort elsewhere.
records.key_question: Where does the next unit of effort stop paying for itself?
records.produces: stop point with the marginal return curve
records.failure_mode: Quitting before the compounding phase, which also looks flat at the start.

records.name: Randomness

origin.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Many outcomes contain a large element of chance. Allow for luck when explaining results, and avoid reading patterns into noise.
records.key_question: Could this outcome be noise?
records.produces: noise-versus-signal verdict
records.failure_mode: Attributing everything to luck, which dissolves accountability entirely.

records.name: Regression to the Mean

origin.author: Francis Galton
origin.work: Regression towards Mediocrity in Hereditary Stature
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: An extreme result is usually followed by one closer to average, because chance contributed to the extreme. Do not credit or blame an intervention for that return.
records.key_question: Was this extreme, and what is the expected next value without any intervention?
use_when: after a record quarter or a disaster
records.produces: adjusted expectation and counterfactual baseline
records.failure_mode: Calling a genuine trend regression to the mean.

records.name: Surface Area

origin.author: Geometry; Scott Page
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: The more exposure you have, the more interactions occur, for good and ill. Increase it to gain ideas and opportunities; reduce it to limit risk.
records.key_question: Do I need more exposure to luck and ideas, or less exposure to risk and attack?
records.produces: exposure decision with the asymmetry stated
records.failure_mode: Increasing exposure beyond the capacity to absorb its consequences.

records.name: Global and Local Maxima

origin.author: Sewall Wright
origin.work: The Roles of Mutation, Inbreeding, Crossbreeding and Selection in Evolution (fitness landscapes)
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: A position can be the best within reach and still well below the best available. Climbing higher may require going downhill first to explore elsewhere.
records.key_question: Am I on a small hill, and what descent is required to reach the larger one?
records.produces: local versus global assessment and cost of descent
records.failure_mode: Abandoning a good position for an imagined better one with no evidence it exists.

records.name: Supply and Demand

origin.author: Alfred Marshall
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Prices move to balance how much people want something against how much is available. Shortages raise prices and draw in supply; gluts do the reverse.
records.key_question: What happens to price and allocation as each side moves?
records.produces: price and allocation forecast with induced responses
records.failure_mode: Static analysis that ignores the supply response your own action provokes.

records.name: Trade-offs

origin.author: Friedrich von Wieser
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Choosing one option gives up the others. The true cost of a choice is the best alternative forgone, so name what you are giving up.
records.key_question: What am I giving up, and is it worth less than what I am getting?
use_when: any allocation of time or capital
records.produces: explicit cost ledger of the foregone option
records.failure_mode: False dilemma: treating compatible options as mutually exclusive.

records.name: Specialization
records.evidence_note: Gains from specialisation are well documented in trade and labour economics. They shrink with coordination costs and rise in fragility when demand shifts.

origin.author: Adam Smith
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Concentrating on a narrow field builds depth and efficiency, at the cost of flexibility. Specialists gain within their domain and are exposed when it changes.
records.key_question: Does this environment reward depth or adaptability right now?
records.produces: depth versus breadth call with the obsolescence risk
records.failure_mode: Specialising into a domain that is being eliminated while you are perfecting it.

records.name: Efficiency
records.evidence_note: Waste reduction raises output in many measured settings (lean studies); the same literature shows removing slack can raise fragility. Evidence is context-specific.

origin.author: Frederick Winslow Taylor
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Efficiency is producing the result with the least waste. Pushed to the limit, it removes the slack a system needs to cope with surprises.
records.key_question: Is this efficiency buying speed today at the price of survival tomorrow?
records.produces: efficiency-resilience balance with the shock scenario
records.failure_mode: Efficiency treated as an unconditional good rather than a bet on stability.

records.name: Debt
records.evidence_note: Leverage amplifies gains and losses by arithmetic; links between debt levels and crises are documented (Reinhart and Rogoff, disputed in method). Causality is contested.

origin.author: Hyman Minsky
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Borrowing brings future resources into the present in exchange for a later obligation with interest. It amplifies outcomes and reduces room for error.
records.key_question: What future obligation am I creating, and what happens if conditions shift?
records.produces: obligation schedule plus fragility check
records.failure_mode: Ignoring non-financial debt: technical, reputational, sleep, goodwill.

records.name: Creative Destruction
records.evidence_note: Productivity growth from firm entry and exit is measured widely (Foster, Haltiwanger and Krizan). How fast incumbents are displaced varies by industry.

origin.author: Joseph Schumpeter
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: New products, firms and methods replace old ones, freeing resources for new uses. No position is permanent, including the incumbent's.
records.key_question: What part of my position is about to be made obsolete, and by what?
records.produces: obsolescence candidates ranked by proximity
records.failure_mode: Destroying functioning systems for novelty, mistaking churn for renewal.

records.name: Plot

origin.author: Aristotle
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: A plot is a chain of events linked by cause, usually driven by conflict toward a resolution. Stories organise facts into this shape whether or not reality has it.
records.key_question: What does the protagonist want, what blocks it, and what follows causally?
use_when: making sense of your own situation
records.produces: causal chain with the central conflict named
records.failure_mode: Imposing narrative causality on events that were substantially random.

records.name: Character
records.evidence_note: Person-situation research (Mischel; Ross and Nisbett) shows behaviour under pressure reveals dispositions only partly. Use as a prompt to read choices, not as a trait test.

origin.author: Robert McKee
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Character is the pattern of choices a person makes, most visible under pressure. It explains behaviour that persists across very different situations.
records.key_question: What do their past choices under pressure predict about the next one?
records.produces: behavioural prediction grounded in specific past choices
records.failure_mode: Fixing a person permanently in a read of who they were at one moment.

records.name: Setting
records.evidence_note: Environment effects on behaviour are well supported (Lewin's field theory; default and choice-architecture studies). Nudge effects are smaller in large replications.

origin.author: Kurt Lewin
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: The environment sets what is easy, hard or possible. Changing the setting often changes behaviour more reliably than appealing to motivation.
records.key_question: What in the environment is producing this behaviour?
records.produces: environmental levers ranked by effect size
records.failure_mode: Environment as total excuse, erasing agency and accountability.

records.name: Seeing the Front

origin.author: Carl von Clausewitz
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Reports pass through filters and delays. Where it matters and is possible, go and see the situation yourself before relying on second-hand accounts.
records.key_question: Have I observed this directly, or only through people with a stake in the report?
records.produces: direct-observation plan and what it would verify
records.failure_mode: Micromanagement dressed as direct observation; the front cannot be everywhere.

records.name: Two-Front War

origin.author: Military history
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Fighting on two fronts at once splits resources and attention. Avoid it yourself, and look for ways to make a rival face it.
records.key_question: Am I splitting force across fronts, and can I close one?
records.produces: front consolidation plan with sequencing
records.failure_mode: Framing independent efforts as 'fronts' to justify abandoning one.

records.name: Mutually Assured Destruction

origin.author: Thomas Schelling
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: When each side can inflict unacceptable damage on the other, both are deterred from attacking. The stability depends on both sides perceiving the threat accurately.
records.key_question: Would using this destroy me as well, and does that change anyone's behaviour?
records.produces: deterrence assessment plus tail-risk if deterrence fails
records.failure_mode: Relying on rational restraint in a system that only needs one error.

records.name: Trust
records.evidence_note: Trust and economic outcomes correlate across countries (Knack and Keefer 1997; Fukuyama 1995). The direction of causation is debated.

origin.author: Francis Fukuyama
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Trust lets people and systems cooperate without checking everything, which lowers costs. It is built slowly and lost quickly, so extend it where it is warranted.
records.key_question: What is the cheapest reliable evidence of trustworthiness here?
records.produces: trust decision with its verification mechanism
records.failure_mode: Trust extended with no verification, which is not trust but hope.

records.name: Liking/Loving and Disliking/Hating
records.evidence_note: Liking colours judgment: halo effect (Thorndike 1920; Nisbett and Wilson 1977) and similarity-liking findings. Effect sizes vary.

origin.author: Charlie Munger
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: We overrate people and things we like and underrate those we dislike, including the evidence they bring. Separate the messenger from the message.
records.key_question: Would I reach this judgement if someone I dislike had said it?
records.produces: source-blind re-evaluation
records.failure_mode: Overcorrecting against people you like, which is the same error signed differently.

records.name: Availability Heuristic
records.evidence_note: Tversky and Kahneman (1973) showed judged frequency tracks ease of recall. Later work refines the mechanism (ease versus content); the core effect replicates.

origin.author: Amos Tversky; Daniel Kahneman
origin.work: Availability: A Heuristic for Judging Frequency and Probability
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: We judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Recent, vivid or frequent events feel more probable than they are.
records.key_question: Is this vivid because it is frequent, or frequent-seeming because it is vivid?
records.produces: frequency correction against actual data
records.failure_mode: Dismissing recent evidence precisely because it is recent.

records.name: Failure to Account for Base Rates

origin.author: Daniel Kahneman; Amos Tversky
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Before judging a specific case, start from how often outcomes like it happen in general. Vivid details tempt us to ignore those background frequencies.
records.key_question: What is the historical frequency for cases like this, before I look at this case's specifics?
records.produces: reference class and the prior it implies
records.failure_mode: Choosing the reference class that produces the conclusion you wanted.

records.name: Tendency to Stereotype
records.evidence_note: Categorical judgment is documented in social cognition. Accuracy of stereotypes is a disputed research area (Jussim); use as a warning about shortcuts, not a verdict on any group.

origin.author: Walter Lippmann
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Sorting people and things into categories saves effort but erases individual differences. Check whether the category actually predicts anything about this case.
records.key_question: Am I using a category where individuating evidence is actually available?
records.produces: specificity check: what individuating data exists
records.failure_mode: Refusing all categorisation, which discards genuine base-rate information.

records.name: Failure to See False Conjunctions

origin.author: Amos Tversky; Daniel Kahneman
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: A detailed scenario can feel more likely than a broader one that contains it, though it cannot be. Each added detail lowers the probability.
records.key_question: Am I rating a detailed scenario as more likely than the broader case that contains it?
records.produces: probability correction toward the parent category
records.failure_mode: Rejecting useful specificity in planning because it is technically less probable.

records.name: Social Proof
records.evidence_note: Conformity (Asch 1951) and informational social influence replicate, with size varying by culture, group size and task.

origin.author: Robert Cialdini
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: We take others' behaviour as evidence of what is right, especially when unsure. Check whether the crowd has independent evidence or is copying itself.
records.key_question: Am I believing this because of evidence, or because of who else believes it?
records.produces: independent evidence check separate from consensus
records.failure_mode: Contrarianism as identity: rejecting consensus because it is consensus.

records.name: Narrative Instinct
records.evidence_note: Narrative fallacy is argued by Taleb from cases; related support exists in explanation-seeking studies. Direct tests of the claimed bias are limited.

origin.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: We understand events as stories with causes, characters and meaning. Stories are memorable and persuasive, which makes them easy to accept without checking.
records.key_question: Is this a story fitted to a known outcome, or an explanation that would have predicted it?
records.produces: separation of narrative from predictive evidence
records.failure_mode: Rejecting narrative entirely; it remains how humans are actually persuaded.

records.name: Curiosity Instinct

origin.author: George Loewenstein
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: People are driven to explore and understand, beyond immediate need. Curiosity opens new options and can pull attention away from the task.
records.key_question: What would I ask if there were no cost to being wrong?
records.produces: exploration list of unasked questions
records.failure_mode: Curiosity as sanctioned procrastination.

records.name: Relative Satisfaction/Misery
records.evidence_note: Income comparison affects reported well-being (Easterlin 1974; Luttmer 2005). Whether absolute income also matters is disputed (Stevenson and Wolfers 2008).

origin.author: Richard Easterlin
origin.work: Does Economic Growth Improve the Human Lot?
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Satisfaction depends on comparison with expectations, past experience and other people more than on absolute conditions. A better situation can feel worse.
records.key_question: Compared to what, and who chose that comparison?
records.produces: named comparison set and its alternatives
records.failure_mode: Dismissing real problems as 'merely relative'.

records.name: Commitment and Consistency Bias
records.evidence_note: Cognitive dissonance findings (Festinger 1957) and foot-in-the-door effects are documented; several classic paradigms replicate with smaller effects than first reported.

origin.author: Leon Festinger
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Once people commit, publicly or privately, they tend to act consistently with it even when evidence changes. Revisit commitments as if making them fresh.
records.key_question: Am I holding this because it is right, or because I already said it?
records.produces: reassessment made independent of prior commitment
records.failure_mode: Abandoning commitments the moment they become costly, which destroys trust.

records.name: Overestimate Consistency of Behavior
records.evidence_note: Correspondence bias (Jones and Harris 1967; Ross 1977) replicates; strength differs across cultures. Behaviour has stable and situational components.

origin.author: Lee Ross
origin.work: The Intuitive Psychologist and His Shortcomings
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: We attribute others' behaviour to their personality and underweight the situation they were in. The same person can act very differently in different contexts.
records.key_question: Trait or situation: what would I conclude if I could only see the context?
records.produces: situational alternative explanation alongside the trait one
records.failure_mode: Excusing repeated behaviour as situational when the pattern is the evidence.

records.name: Influence of Stress
records.evidence_note: Acute stress impairs prefrontal function and shifts people toward habit in laboratory studies (Arnsten 2009; Schwabe and Wolf). Evidence is mostly acute-stress lab work.

origin.author: Amy Arnsten
origin.work: Stress signalling pathways that impair prefrontal cortex structure and function
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: Under stress, people fall back on habits and quick reactions and are more open to bias. Expect worse judgment in a crisis and set up decisions in advance.
records.key_question: What state am I deciding from, and what does that state degrade?
records.produces: state check plus deferral rule for reversible decisions
records.failure_mode: Using stress as grounds to dismiss a sound decision that was made under pressure.

records.name: Survivorship Bias

origin.author: Abraham Wald
origin.work: Statistical Research Group memoranda on aircraft survivability
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: We see the cases that survived and miss those that failed, so lessons drawn from survivors alone can be wrong. Look for the missing failures before drawing conclusions.
records.key_question: Where are the ones who did the same thing and failed?
records.produces: missing-losers analysis and what it does to the inference
records.failure_mode: Dismissing all learning from winners; some winners did have a real edge.

records.name: Tendency to Want to Do Something
records.evidence_note: Penalty-kick goalkeepers dive more often than staying put would justify (Bar-Eli et al. 2007). Generalisation to other domains rests on fewer studies.

origin.author: Michael Bar-Eli et al.
origin.work: Action bias among elite soccer goalkeepers
origin.note: Selection follows Farnam Street's Great Mental Models

records.summary: There is a strong pull to act, especially when watched or under pressure, even when waiting would be better. Ask whether action improves the outcome or only relieves discomfort.
records.key_question: Is action required, or am I acting to feel useful?
records.produces: do-nothing option explicitly costed alongside the others
records.failure_mode: Inaction rationalised as discipline when the cost of waiting is the larger risk.
